1_door_walk: chapter 1, a quiet Sunday afternoon in a narrow London by-street. Two Victorian gentlemen walk side by side on the pavement, mid-stride, past a sinister old building. On the left, Mr Utterson the lawyer: a lean, long, dry, dreary man with a rugged unsmiling face, lank dust-fair hair, clean-shaven, a black bowler hat, a sober black suit under a long greatcoat. On the right, Mr Enfield: a younger man about town of thirty-five, brown hair and a neat brown moustache, a fawn overcoat and a grey top hat, pointing with his cane at the building. The building beside them is a two-storey block whose gable juts onto the street: the upper storey a flat blank wall of discoloured plaster, a single blistered, paint-stained door below, set in a recess at the top of two worn stone steps, neither bell nor knocker. Grey overcast daylight, thin fog, wet cobbles, soot-blackened brick.
2_trampling: chapter 1, three o'clock on a black winter morning at a deserted London street corner under one gas lamp. Mr Edward Hyde, a small, stooped, pale man, hunched and coiled, with a sinister sneering grin, coarse black hair and short coarse black side-whiskers, wearing a low-crowned soft black felt hat and a badly fitting dark coat, strides heavily forward and does not stop; a little girl of eight in a pale pinafore has fallen on the cobbles at his feet and looks up at him, frightened. A moment of cold menace: his shadow falls over her, his face lit from below by the gas lamp. Fog, black empty street, shuttered shopfronts, deep shadow.
3_fireside: chapter 3, a comfortable Victorian drawing room at night, warm firelight. Dr Henry Jekyll sits in a deep leather armchair on the right of the fireplace: a large, well-made, smooth-faced man of fifty, plainly middle-aged, with thick iron-grey hair, grey at the temples, lines about the eyes, clean-shaven, in a good dark frock coat and waistcoat, holding a glass of wine, smiling kindly. Opposite him on the left sits Mr Utterson the lawyer, lean and long with a rugged unsmiling face, lank dust-fair hair, clean-shaven, in a sober black suit. Between them a carved oak mantel, a low fire, a decanter on a small table, books, dark panelled walls. Two men only.
4_carew: chapter 4, the Carew murder: a narrow London lane at night drowned in thick brown fog under a full moon. A small, stooped figure, Mr Edward Hyde, seen almost in silhouette against the fog-glow of a gas lamp, in a low-crowned soft black felt hat and a badly fitting coat, raises a heavy walking cane high above his head with both hands, coiled to strike. In front of him, half turned away, an old white-haired gentleman in a dark coat lifts a hand. No blood, no gore; a frozen moment of menace. Wet cobbles, black railings, a moonlit fog bank.
5_lanyon: chapter 6, the study of Dr Hastie Lanyon at night. Dr Lanyon sits alone at his desk, a stout, healthy, dapper, red-faced gentleman of fifty with a shock of prematurely white hair, but now stricken: his ruddy face gone grey and pale, eyes wide and haunted, one hand gripping the desk edge, an untouched lamp beside him. A single oil lamp lights him from the side; tall shelves of medical books and a skull on a shelf behind him in deep shadow. One man only.
6_cabinet_door: chapter 8, the last night: a dim stone corridor at the top of a short flight of stairs, lit by one candle. Before a closed red baize cabinet door stand two men. Poole the butler: a well-dressed, elderly, stout servant with grey mutton-chop whiskers, a bald crown, a black tailcoat and white neckcloth, both hands gripping a heavy woodsman's axe raised over his shoulder, ready to swing. Beside him Mr Utterson the lawyer, lean and long with a rugged unsmiling face, lank dust-fair hair, clean-shaven, in a black greatcoat, holding a poker, tense. Their long shadows climb the wall; a thin line of light under the door. Two men only.
